# Signed BIGINT amount in cents: positive = credit, negative = debit

> The `amount` field stores money in cents as a signed integer: positive for credits (money in), negative for debits (money out).

_Part of [Immutable ledger entry row](ledger-entry-row.md)_

Every line in the ledger (a [Immutable ledger entry row](ledger-entry-row.md)) has an `amount`—a single number that is positive or negative. Positive means money came in (a credit); negative means money went out (a debit). Using a signed integer is mathematically cleaner than keeping separate `debit` and `credit` columns; you just add all the amounts up, and they must sum to zero. The amount is always in cents, never dollars. So $1.00 is stored as `100`, not `1`. This keeps all numbers as integers and dodges the floating-point rounding errors that break financial systems. Once an entry is written, its amount is immutable—you can never update it. If you make a mistake, you post a reversal entry instead. The [Recording money in the ledger](recording-money-in-ledger.md) process enforces that every journal balances: debits and credits are just the sign of the amount.

**Look at:** [`amount` in ledger-entry.model.ts](../../../../packages/backend/libs/domains/payments/infra/models/ledger-entry.model.ts#L50)

## What it touches

| Kind | Name | How |
|---|---|---|
| database | `LedgerEntry.amount` | A BIGINT column storing the signed amount in cents for each journal line; the database enforces that all lines in a journal sum to zero. |

## Watch out

- Stored in cents, not dollars—$1.00 is `100`, not `1`; raw DB values look deceptively small.
- Immutable once posted—errors cannot be fixed by updating an amount; you must post a reversal entry.
- Every journal must sum to zero—the database rejects any set of entries that don't balance, even if off by one cent.
